To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the brain regions involved in making choices and in forming beliefs are different, and the brain regions involved when forming 2nd-order (self-referential) beliefs are a mixture of the regions used for making choices and forming beliefs.

the neural correlates of strategic thinking in games are (i) cingulate cortex and (ii) prefrontal areas, and (iii) that equilibrium is a “state of the mind,” with little difference in neural activation across choice and belief games, and (iv) that the insula may be the seat of strategic IQ, and that ventral striatal activation is positively associated with it.

the cingulate and prefrontal cortex are differentially activated when subjects make choices versus express beliefs, and that in equilibrium, there is no difference in neural activity in these areas across choice and belief conditions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the mind works in games and how it can be used to define equilibrium.
understanding how people make choices, form beliefs, and express beliefs in strategic games.
the neural basis of equilibrium and strategic thinking, and how the brain implements social reasoning and strategic behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
“self-referential thinking and equilibrium are states of mind.”
there are neural signatures of equilibrium and of strategic IQ.
there is a strong neural basis for the concept of equilibrium as a state of mind, and that the neural basis of equilibrium is different from that of the processes that generate it.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain is not a computer that computes, but rather an organ that computes in a way that reflects its evolutionary history and its current state of health.
“equilibrium” is not just a mathematical concept, but also a psychological and neural state.
the neural basis of strategic thinking in games is a complex mixture of social cognition and decision-making.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a neural basis for equilibrium in games and for the notion of “strategic IQ” that is independent of actual earnings.
the brain can be used to understand strategic thinking, and vice versa, and that there is a purely neuroscientific definition of equilibrium.
there is a purely neurobiological definition of equilibrium as states of mind.
